title: Legendre polynomials: irreducibility and all signed permutations
summary: Two preprints claim all-degree irreducibility and the full group \(C_2\wr S_m\), combining resultant estimates with local cycles and the action on opposite root pairs.
scope: Over \(\mathbb Q\), for every \(m\ge1\) and \(\delta\in\{0,1\}\), with the standard normalization \(P_n(1)=1\) and \(L_{2m+\delta}(x)=P_{2m+\delta}(x)/x^\delta\). Both all-degree inputs remain preprint claims.

body:
Preprint claims in every degree. Put \(L_{2m+\delta}(x)=P_{2m+\delta}(x)/x^\delta=Q_{m,\delta}(x^2)\), where \(m\ge1\) and \(\delta\in\{0,1\}\). Deng’s version 2 claims that \(L_{2m+\delta}\) is irreducible. Nguyen-Dang’s version 1 claims the complete group determination

\[\operatorname{Gal}(Q_{m,\delta}/\mathbb Q)=S_m,\qquad \operatorname{Gal}(L_{2m+\delta}/\mathbb Q)=C_2^m\rtimes S_m.\]

The latter group acts on \(2m\) roots: \(S_m\) permutes opposite pairs, and \(C_2^m\) exchanges their members independently. Irreducibility alone does not determine either group. The two AND nodes show the extra inputs required.

The resultant comparison excludes factors in large degree; a finite completion is part of the irreducibility claim. On the group side, local cycles first determine the action on pairs. For \(m\ge4\), an odd proper pair flip and its conjugates generate every sign change; the three smaller pair degrees receive explicit checks.

Why the resultant bounds conflict

For \(n=2m+\delta\), write \(2^{v_2(n!)}P_n(x)/x^\delta=H(x^2)\). Deng’s Lemma 2.2 makes every rational factor of \(2^{v_2(n!)}P_n(x)/x^\delta\) even, so every proper factorization descends to \(H=AB\). For a nontrivial factorization, take \(1\le k=\deg A\le m/2\), and let \(R_{\mathrm{odd}}\) be the positive odd part of \(|\operatorname{Res}(A,B)|\). For \(n\ge64\), the Wronskian identity and orthogonality give the upper bound below; Legendre’s differential equation and Chebyshev–Hadamard estimates give the lower bound:

\[m\log4-\log\!\frac{4(m+1)^2}{\sqrt m}<\frac{\log R_{\mathrm{odd}}}{k}<\bigl(m+\sqrt{2n-1}\bigr)\log3.\]

These bounds contradict each other for \(n\ge256\); the finite completion covers \(2\le n\le255\) (Deng, Theorems 4.1, 5.1 and §6).

The source statements and these dependencies were checked. The full preprint proofs have not been independently verified, and the all-degree conclusions retain the status Claimed.

title: Four Jacobi families: modular forms, symmetric groups, and Jacobians
summary: The Kaneko–Zagier families connect modular polynomial factors to an all-degree symmetric-group claim; Zarhin’s published theorem then controls the associated hyperelliptic Jacobians.
scope: For \(f=P_n^{(\lambda/3,\mu/2)}\) over \(\mathbb Q\), \(n\ge1\), \(\lambda,\mu\in\{\pm1\}\). The Galois assertion is a preprint claim; the Jacobian consequence requires \(n\ge5\) and that assertion.

edges.explanation: The four Jacobi polynomials become Kaneko–Zagier modular factors under the stated rational affine substitution and scaling.

edges.explanation: The preprint claims irreducibility and the full symmetric group for each of the four families in every positive degree.

edges.explanation: The distinct roots of f are the finite branch points of the smooth projective model of y²=f(x).

edges.explanation: The symmetric-group input is the preprint-dependent hypothesis for this application.

edges.explanation: For a characteristic-zero polynomial of degree at least five with group Sₙ or Aₙ, Zarhin proves that every geometric Jacobian endomorphism is integer multiplication.

edges.explanation: A nontrivial abelian subvariety would give an idempotent in the rational endomorphism algebra, whereas End⁰=Q has only 0 and 1.

body:
Let \(f=P_n^{(\lambda/3,\mu/2)}\), with \(n\ge1\) and \(\lambda,\mu\in\{\pm1\}\). Theorem 1.1 of the 2026 Jacobi preprint claims that every such polynomial is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\) and has group \(S_n\).

The published modular identification is exact. Put \(\ell=12n+6+2\lambda+3\mu\). The corresponding Kaneko–Zagier factor is

\[\widetilde F_{\ell-1}(Y)=1728^n f(1-Y/864).\]

This rational affine substitution preserves the splitting field. If \(\ell\) is prime, the monic supersingular \(j\)-polynomial satisfies

\[S_\ell(Y)\equiv Y^{(\lambda+1)/2}(Y-1728)^{(\mu+1)/2}\,\widetilde F_{\ell-1}(Y)\pmod\ell.\]

The two exponents record whether the supersingular invariants \(0\) and \(1728\) occur. The prime-index requirement belongs to this modular reduction, not to the characteristic-zero Galois claim.

Now suppose \(n\ge5\), and let \(C\) be the smooth projective model of \(y^2=f(x)\). Its genus is \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\). Combining the claimed group \(S_n\) with Zarhin’s published theorem gives

\[\operatorname{End}_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}(\operatorname{Jac}C)=\mathbb Z.\]

Thus the Jacobian is absolutely simple. This application retains the preprint dependency even though Zarhin’s implication is established. Irreducibility by itself would not provide its group hypothesis.

title: Legendre values: from prime divisibility to base-p digits
summary: A published all-degree formula expresses \(v_p(P_n(p))\) through central binomial coefficients and gives a recurrence that reads the base-p digits of n.
scope: Standard Legendre polynomials, every odd prime \(p\), and every integer \(n\ge0\). The evaluation point is the same prime p as the valuation; the distinct p=2 formula is stated below.

edges.explanation: The coefficient estimates identify one summand with strictly smaller p-adic valuation in the relevant parity expansion.

edges.explanation: The least-valuation term gives the displayed formulas for even and odd degrees without cancellation.

edges.label: Kummer’s carry formula
edges.explanation: The valuation of the central binomial coefficient equals the number of carries in the base-p addition m+m.

edges.label: Legendre’s factorial formula
edges.explanation: Writing factorial valuations as digit sums gives the all-degree digit formula in Theorem 4.

edges.explanation: Splitting n into its last base-p digit and remaining prefix yields the two-case recurrence.

edges.explanation: The recurrence evaluates fₚ(n) using the digits of n and the parity of each prefix.

edges.explanation: The binomial identity Pₙ(3)=Σⱼ binom(n,j)binom(n+j,j) identifies the central Delannoy sequence.

body:
Let \(f_p(n)=v_p(P_n(p))\), where \(p\ge3\) is prime and \(P_n(1)=1\). For every \(m\ge0\), the published theorem gives

\[f_p(2m)=v_p\binom{2m}{m},\qquad f_p(2m+1)=1+v_p(2m+1)+v_p\binom{2m}{m}.\]

Kummer identifies the binomial valuation with carries in \(m+m\) in base \(p\). Equivalently, if \(s_p(n)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits,

\[f_p(n)=\frac{2s_p(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)-s_p(n)+(n\bmod2)p}{p-1}.\]

For every \(n\ge0\) and \(0\le a\[f_p(pn+a)=\begin{cases}f_p(n)+(n\bmod2),&a\text{ even},\\f_p(n)+1-(n\bmod2),&a\text{ odd}.\end{cases}\]

At \(p=3\), \(P_n(3)\) is the central Delannoy number. Since \(13=(111)_3\), the recurrence gives \(f_3(1)=1\), \(f_3(4)=1\), and \(f_3(13)=2\); indeed \(P_{13}(3)=1409933619=9\cdot156659291\), with the last factor prime to \(3\).

The prime \(2\) has its own formula: \(v_2(P_n(2))=(n\bmod2)-v_2(n!)\). These are valuation theorems in every degree, not irreducibility criteria.
